title: The Irrelevant Sound Effect on Serial Recall Is Independent of Age and Inhibitory Control
research_question: To test for developmental differences in susceptibility to classroom noise while taking individual inhibitory control into account, specifically examining the effects of irrelevant sound on serial and non-serial memory tasks across different age groups and its association with inhibitory control.

participants.description: Younger children (8-10 years, n=57, M=9.2, SD=0.6, 35 female), Older children (11-12 years, n=73, M=11.3, SD=1.0, 44 female), Young adults (19-32 years, n=52, M=23.6, SD=3.2, 39 female). Participants were from Germany.
participants.recruitment: Recruited in middle-class schools and at the university via leaflets, informative letters, and e-mails.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Classroom noise, consisting of 13 different sound tracks (8-25 sec long) presented in randomized order. Sounds were actual classroom noise, mainly group work, with bits of English conversation. Presented at 55-60 dB(A).

measures.instrument: Proportion correct of visually presented digit sequences recalled in correct order
Proportion correct of visually presented noun-pairs recalled (order within pair not relevant)
Stroop Task (difference in reaction times between incongruent and congruent trials)

findings.quote: serial recall performance was similarly impaired by classroom noise in all three age-groups.
disruption by classroom noise was not evident in paired-associative recall in any age group.
Individual susceptibility to the detrimental noise impact was neither associated with age nor with inhibitory control

findings.antecedent: Age group x Sound condition x Memory task
findings.quote: the three-way interaction of age group, sound condition and task (F< 1) was not significant
interaction between age group and sound condition (F< 1) was not significant

findings.antecedent: Sound condition (silence vs. classroom noise) x Memory task (serial vs. paired-associate recall)
findings.quote: significant interaction between sound condition and task (F(1,179) = 12.19, p < .001, partial n² = .06)
disturbance effect of classroom noise in serial recall task (t(182) = 4.21, p < .001, Cohen's d = .44)
classroom noise had no effect on recall accuracy in paired-associate recall (t(182) = .90, p = .38,, Cohen's d = .09)
main effect of sound condition (classroom noise vs. silence) was also significant (F(1,179) = 28.65, p < .001; partial n² = .14) with an overall higher performance in silence
interaction between age group and task was also significant (F(2,179) = 17.46, p < .001, partial n² = .16)

findings.antecedent: Age group (young adults > older children > younger children)
findings.quote: In paired-associate recall, young adults performed significantly better than older children (t(123) = 6.5, p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.6), who performed significantly better than younger children (t(128) = 6.62, p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.17).

findings.antecedent: Age group (young adults > older children, young adults > younger children)
findings.quote: In serial recall, young adults performed significantly better than older children (t(123) = 2.67, p < .01, Cohen's d = 0.5) and younger children (t(107) = 3.03, p < .01, Cohen´s d = 0.6)

findings.antecedent: Age group (older children vs. younger children)
findings.quote: Older and younger children did not differ significantly in serial recall performance (t(128) = 0.50, p = .61, Cohen's d = 0.05).
findings._quarantine_reason: Value 0.05 appears to be a p-value, not an effect size

findings.quote: Overall, the main effect of age was significant (F(2,179) = 43.15, p < .001, partial n² = .32).
The main effect of task was not significant (F< 1), indicating comparable overall difficulty of the two memory tasks.

mechanisms: Interference-by-process: Irrelevant sounds disrupt cognitive performance by drawing on the same processes or functions as the volitional task (e.g., order information encoding for changing-state sounds interfering with serial recall).
Attentional capture: Irrelevant sounds disrupt cognitive performance by capturing attention and redirecting it from the task-relevant information.
moderators: Age group (younger children, older children, young adults)
Memory task type (serial recall vs. paired-associate recall)
implementation_implications: The detrimental impact of classroom noise on serial recall is consistent across age groups (8-32 years), suggesting that children are as susceptible as adults to this type of interference.

The effect of classroom noise is task-specific, primarily affecting tasks requiring serial order retention (like serial recall) but not non-serial tasks (like paired-associate recall). This implies that educational strategies should consider the type of cognitive task when assessing noise impact.

Individual differences in inhibitory control, as measured by the Stroop task, do not generally predict susceptibility to irrelevant sound effects across all age groups, except for a positive correlation in young adults (higher Stroop interference associated with stronger noise impact).

tables.description: Mean performance (M) and standard deviation (SD) in three age groups and in all tasks for Serial Recall (pc), Paired-associate Recall (pc), and Stroop (RTs). Includes Difference A and Baseline corrected A for each measure.

limitations: The sample size within each age group (N < 100) limits the interpretation of correlation findings between detrimental noise impact and Stroop interference within those groups.
The classroom noise stimuli might have lacked sufficient quantity and quality of 'deviants' to trigger a strong attentional capture effect, potentially underestimating the role of attention.
Daily exposure to classroom noise and potential habituation in children might have occluded age-related differences in susceptibility to noise.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Changes in auditory stimuli disrupt the processing of serially ordered information in working memory, leading to impaired serial recall, and the paper investigates if this effect is independent of age and inhibitory control.

mechanism_chain.description: Changing-state irrelevant sounds capture attention and interfere with the phonological loop's ability to process order information, thereby impairing serial recall performance.

steps.to_construct: attentional capture / disruption of order processing

steps.from_construct: attentional capture / disruption of order processing

instruments_used.name: Serial Recall Task
instruments_used.construct: verbal working memory / serial order processing
instruments_used.description: Participants are presented with a list of items (e.g., digits, words) and asked to recall them in the exact order of presentation.

instruments_used.name: Inhibitory Control Task
instruments_used.description: A task designed to measure the ability to suppress prepotent responses or irrelevant information (e.g., Stroop task, Flanker task).
